The benthic amphipod Corophium volutator exhibits a clearly definable size at birth, with newly eclosed juveniles emerging from the maternal brood pouch at a body length of just 0.1 cm [Lb = 0.1 cm]. This diminutive starting size reflects the species’ reliance on yolk reserves during the earliest post-embryonic stages, a common pattern among tube-dwelling infaunal crustaceans that colonize intertidal mudflats. Laboratory-reared individuals maintained under stable conditions demonstrate that eclosion occurs after a brief developmental period; at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth is approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. This relatively rapid embryonic development positions C. volutator as a species capable of exploiting ephemeral sedimentary habitats, where the ability to quickly transition from the brood pouch to active deposit feeding confers a clear competitive advantage over slower-developing co-occurring macrofauna.

As juveniles grow and progress through successive molts, the transition to sexual maturity is marked by the attainment of a specific body length. Field surveys and controlled mesocosm studies consistently indicate that C. volutator reaches puberty at a body length of 0.5 cm [Lp = 0.5 cm], a metric that correlates strongly with the onset of gonadal development and the differentiation of secondary sexual characteristics. This size threshold is ecologically significant, as it aligns with the point at which individuals begin to invest energy into reproductive structures rather than solely into somatic growth. In comparison to its congener Corophium arenarium, which matures at a slightly larger size in similar sedimentary environments, the pubertal length of C. volutator reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output, a trait advantageous in highly dynamic intertidal zones subject to frequent disturbance and predation pressure from migratory shorebirds.

Beyond the pubertal milestone, sexually mature adults continue to increase in size until they approach their ultimate physical length, which has been documented as 1.05 cm [Li = 1.05 cm] based on extensive morphometric sampling of populations from the Wadden Sea. This asymptotic size represents the maximum body length achievable under optimal environmental conditions, after which growth plateaus and energetic resources are diverted predominantly toward reproduction and somatic maintenance. Interestingly, the ultimate physical length is more than double the length at puberty, indicating a prolonged period of post-maturational growth that allows older, larger females to produce larger broods. Such a pattern is consistent with the reproductive biology of many gammaridean amphipods, where fecundity scales positively with female body size, thereby conferring a selective advantage on individuals that survive multiple reproductive seasons and continue to grow incrementally.

The same captive-rearing experiments conducted at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] also revealed key life-history timing parameters. The time to first reproduction, defined as the interval from eclosion to the first appearance of fully developed gonads, was recorded at 29 days after hatching [tR = 29 days after hatching] under these thermal conditions at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This relatively early maturation, occurring less than a month post-hatching, underscores the opportunistic life-history strategy of C. volutator, which is adapted to the short, productive summers characteristic of north-temperate intertidal flats. Furthermore, the species exhibits a maximum adult lifespan of 365 days [am = 365 days] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that permits multiple reproductive bouts over a single year. This annual lifespan places C. volutator at the shorter end of the spectrum among marine amphipods, yet it is sufficient to sustain dense local populations through continuous recruitment during the warmer months.

Reproductive output in C. volutator is strongly influenced by both body size and environmental temperature. Ovigerous females produce successive broods throughout the breeding season, and the maximum reproductive output has been estimated under constant laboratory conditions. At a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females may produce multiple broods, with each brood containing a certain number of offspring. In terms of dry mass, the ultimate dry weight of a fully grown adult has been measured at 0.006594 grams , representing the peak somatic mass achievable when food resources are abundant. This modest dry weight, equivalent to just a few milligrams, reflects the small body size of this species and its efficient allocation of ingested organic material toward rapid growth and repeated reproduction, ensuring population persistence in a challenging, predation-rich intertidal environment.
